item.title: China's resilience exposes limits of US tariff policy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
A tariff intended to exert pressure abroad is still a tax collected at home. The Sino-US trade dispute has illustrated the difficulty of imposing costs on a major economic partner without imposing them on one's own firms and consumers. China's resilience has exposed the limits of a tariff diplomacy. Resilience matters, but its lasting value depends on translating industrial strength into broadly shared prosperity at home and building more stable economic relationships abroad. Both require continued domestic reform and sustained international cooperation. September's agreement to extend the trade truce to Jan 10 offers an opening. The two governments also advanced a framework for more favorable tariff treatment covering approximately $30 billion of goods in each direction, subject to domestic legal procedures. Differences over technology, industrial policy and economic security will require sustained consultation. An assessment of tariff diplomacy begins with who bears its costs. Research published in October by economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University found that nearly 90 percent of the tariff increases studied passed through to tariff-inclusive US import prices, using data through February 2026. The burden is subsequently distributed through business margins, supply chains and retail prices. US manufacturers relying on imported components face higher costs alongside their customers. Protection conferred on one industry can impose a disadvantage on another. Tariffs can redirect purchases and shelter particular producers. Lasting competitiveness, however, requires skills, technology, infrastructure and suppliers. Raising the price of competing imports cannot, by itself, bring these capabilities into existence. China's manufacturing strength, above all, rests on an ecosystem accumulated over decades. Supplier networks, skilled workers, engineering expertise, infrastructure and production at scale reinforce one another. Their interaction helps firms resolve production problems and bring new products to market. A factory may be replaced more readily than the knowledge and relationships that make it productive. Chinese firms have also diversified markets and reorganized production. Final assembly abroad may continue to depend on Chinese machinery, materials and components. Bilateral trade figures reveal only part of this adjustment. Innovation in batteries, renewable energy equipment and digital technologies adds resilience through improvements in quality, efficiency and performance. The interaction between research, engineering and production also creates opportunities for innovation across borders. Appropriate commercial incentives and regulatory conditions could help both economies develop and apply new technologies more efficiently through cooperation. Changing production patterns nevertheless entail adjustment. IMD Business School Professor Richard Baldwin's recent analysis highlights the importance of scale: slower growth from a much larger industrial base can still generate substantial additions to output. The benefits and adjustments associated with that expansion need not be evenly distributed. Cheaper imports can benefit consumers and downstream firms, while particular industries and communities face more concentrated pressures. Concerns about employment and industrial capabilities therefore deserve greater attention in both countries. Workers need support and training, while firms need room to adapt and investment to improve productivity. Given the scale of China's industrial base, sustained industrial success is increasingly tied to the opportunities it creates across economies. Continued dialogue and practical cooperation with trading partners can help those opportunities develop. For China, sustaining resilience requires continued domestic reform. The capacity to produce, the income available to households and the jobs available to workers need to advance together. A stronger domestic market depends on bringing them into closer alignment. Recent data reveal the unevenness of demand. In the first nine months of this year, retail sales of goods rose by 1 percent in nominal terms, while retail sales of services increased by 5 percent. Services offer an important avenue for growth, but stronger household purchasing power remains essential to a broader expansion of demand. Yi Gang, former governor of the People's Bank of China, has emphasized support for young children, better schooling and affordable housing for migrant worker families, and better access to healthcare. These proposals address the longer perspective of household decisions: what must be reserved for future limits what can be spent today. Yu Yongding, a prominent scholar at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, approaches weak demand from another direction. When households await higher incomes and firms await more orders, public infrastructure investment can help break the impasse. It can generate employment, improve business conditions and, by lowering costs, encourage private investment. The enduring case for a public investment project rests partly on the economic activity it makes possible after construction is complete. Its immediate contribution to demand should be assessed alongside its effects on productivity, employment and subsequent incomes. The quality of investment determines how far today's expenditure strengthens tomorrow's economy. Yi's discussion of local government assets draws a useful distinction between an asset's social value and the cash flow available to service its debt. Public investment needs arrangements for repayment and continued operation. Combining capital investment with sustainable funding for public services can support employment, ease household financial pressures and translate public assets into lasting gains in living standards and consumption. Employment policy must also respond to technological change. Harvard Professor Dani Rodrik has argued that China should extend its experience in raising manufacturing productivity to services. Helping smaller service-sector firms improve technology, management and quality can spread productivity gains more widely. More predictable regulations and fairer market access can strengthen private firms' confidence to invest and hire. Economists differ over the roles of income distribution, investment and exchange rates in rebalancing. These debates underline the macroeconomic roots of trade tensions. Tariff negotiations alone cannot address all of them. Trade measures can rearrange bilateral flows without resolving the underlying balance between saving and investment. Lasting adjustments depend partly on domestic choices in economies. Successful domestic adjustments would also strengthen international cooperation. More secure household purchasing power would give Chinese firms a larger home market and foreign businesses new opportunities, supported by transparent and dependable market access. A stronger home market would also give trading partners more scope to benefit from China's growth and accommodate the changes it brings. The rules governing international engagement therefore matter. Competition increasingly concerns subsidies, technical standards, data governance and market access. These arrangements influence investment decisions and determine how firms manage interdependence. Practical cooperation could begin with simpler customs procedures, electronic trade documents and clearer guidance on product classification and origin. Subsidies require greater transparency and regular consultation. Reliable information about objectives, beneficiaries and cross-border effects would permit a fuller assessment of the interests of competing producers, downstream businesses and consumers. Evidence cannot reconcile every policy preference, but it can establish more intelligible grounds for disagreement. Such efforts should build on multilateral rules and remain open to other economies. Security measures need clearly defined purposes and should be proportionate to identifiable risks, preserving sufficient certainty for ordinary commerce, investment and scientific exchanges. Universities and research institutions can bring analytical discipline to debates on supply chains, technology and trade. Sustained exchanges among scholars, businesses and policymakers can distinguish disagreements about evidence from differences of interest, and clarify where accommodation remains possible. A stable Sino-US economic relationship should make adjustments more manageable and prosperity more widely shared. China's resilience offers a firmer basis for domestic reform, while greater predictability would give firms and households in both economies more confidence to invest and plan. Economic strength is ultimately measured by the prosperity it sustains, not the pressure it can exert. The writer is a professor at the University of International Business and Economics. The views do not necessarily reflect those of China Daily.

item.title: Chinese star Lang Ping gets volleyball's highest honor
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
China's volleyball legend Lang Ping, who was awarded the Volleyball Order on Saturday, dedicated the honor to those who helped mold her remarkable career as congratulatory messages poured in. The 65-year-old former Chinese player and coach received the Volleyball Order, the highest recognition of the sport's governing body, FIVB, at the 40th FIVB World Congress in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic. Lang, a legend of the sport who has won Olympic gold medals as a player and coach, was long considered a top contender for the top FIVB award, and yet remained humble in her acceptance speech, attributing her success to teamwork. "When I accepted this important award, I felt all my coaches, former teammates, players and partners I have worked with were standing on the podium with me," Lang shared on her Weibo account early on Sunday morning. "I started playing volleyball in Beijing when I was 14. From my earliest training on the court, to putting on the Chinese national jersey, and then to coaching overseas, I have walked this path with volleyball for 50 years. Every step of this journey, I have traveled with a team," she said. "None of my dreams could have come true without a group of like-minded people striving with me." Looking ahead, Lang expressed her hope of seeing "many more women coaches stand on this stage and more people around the world get to fall in love with volleyball". Known as the "Iron Hammer" in the volleyball world for her stellar playing career as a ferocious outside hitter, Lang spearheaded China's rise on the sport's global stage in the early 1980s, powering the Chinese women's squad with her explosive strikes and exceptional leadership to two World Cup crowns, a world championship trophy and the gold medal at the Los Angeles Olympics in 1984. During the run of international titles, Lang and her teammates triggered a nationwide volleyball craze, turning her nickname into a timeless symbol of grit, unity and fighting spirit, which ignited the nation during a trying time and forged the core value of China's sporting endeavors in the decades that followed. After retiring as an athlete, she built an international coaching resume rarely matched in the sport's history, taking the helm of the Chinese national team in 1995 and guiding her squad to a runner-up finish at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics. Lang then expanded her influence overseas. She accepted an offer in 2005 to take charge of the United States women's team, after a successful stint with multiple Italian clubs at the league level, and led Team USA to a silver-medal finish at the Beijing Olympics in 2008. Lang's coaching career peaked with her second spell at the helm of Team China, where she revived the struggling program and nurtured a group of talented young stars, such as Zhu Ting and Hui Ruoqi, who went in as pre-tournament underdogs, to a gold-medal finish at the 2016 Rio Olympics. By immersing herself in different systems of the sport, Lang stood out as a genuine global ambassador for not just volleyball but also female empowerment in sports, freely exchanging ideas and bridging diverse cultures. "Congratulations, coach Lang, on receiving the FIVB Volleyball Order. From you, we see how the spirit of Chinese women's volleyball can be passed down and take root globally, as well as the wider possibilities open to women," said the now retired Hui, captain of Lang's 2016 Olympic champion team. "I hope your two cherished visions come to fruition: more female coaches stepping onto the world stage and volleyball drawing participants from all walks of life." The Volleyball Order recognizes individuals who have made an exceptional and lasting contribution to the growth and advancement of volleyball and beach volleyball worldwide. The FIVB described Lang as "a global volleyball icon whose achievements as both a player and coach have inspired generations". sunxiaochen@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: NVIDIA board reinstates Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board director
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
SAN FRANCISCO -- US chipmaker NVIDIA announced Monday that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the company's president and chief executive officer (CEO), as well as a member of its board of directors, with immediate effect. In a statement, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead the company. The board also said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," said Harvey C. Jones, chair of the board. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company," he said. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said, cited by the statement. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 amid mounting pressure over his extramarital affairs. Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress was appointed as interim CEO. Under the latest decision, Kress will continue to serve as CFO, while Jones will remain board chairman. "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," US President Donald Trump said on Monday following NVIDIA's announcement.

item.title: COP31 ends without agreement on climate deal
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
The 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31, failed to reach consensus on the Antalya Pact on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye. After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime, COP31 President Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement, confirmed he would not advance any new text, and later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives. "There is nothing to do, we did all that we could. Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision and we will respect their decision," he said. The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009. While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree on a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed upon by previous summits or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change. Many delegates from developing countries arrived in Antalya hoping that COP31 would deliver stronger support for mitigation and adaptation. However, as the negotiations dragged on, those hopes increasingly gave way to frustration. The mood was already visible at Friday night's plenary session, which began after 9 pm, more than an hour late. Shortly after the session opened, a protester interrupted Kurum. Standing on a chair with a red noose around his neck and wearing a shirt that read "You are killing the future", the protester shouted: "There's no money. The Global South cannot wait," and "You are doing nothing, nothing at all." The protester was escorted from the hall by security officers. The scene reflected the deep divisions among the participating countries over fossil fuels, climate finance and the direction of global energy transition. Some NGOs warned that the conference was at risk of becoming one of the most disappointing COPs in recent years. In an open letter to Kurum and Chris Bowen, COP31 president of negotiations, dozens of nongovernmental organizations around the world said: "The Global South is being abandoned." They accused developed countries of blocking progress and coming to the conference without new financial commitments. "Without finance, communities on every front line will be sacrificed," they said. Division over finance Finance remained one of the most difficult issues. An earlier draft included language on tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion a year by 2035. But the second draft removed the explicit target, while the last proposal failed to provide a clear baseline or detailed delivery pathway for adaptation finance. Developing countries had demanded greater clarity on how much money would be provided, by whom and on what terms. The last draft also showed how the presidency sought to avoid a direct confrontation over fossil fuels. It retained a proposal to raise electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. Under the UN climate convention, parties are to periodically assess the adequacy of the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement's goal of holding warming well below 2 C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. The review is intended to consider the latest science, climate impacts that have been observed, and progress in implementing commitments. According to the UNFCCC, the review should take place at least every seven years. Addressing the Friday plenary session, China expressed serious concern that some parties were seeking to weaken or end the mechanism in the name of streamlining and efficiency. It said the review was an established process and called on parties to discuss the timing and modalities of the third review at COP32, while drawing on the latest scientific findings and avoiding duplication with the global stocktake, a comprehensive assessment of the progress made in achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement. Speaking for the Arab Group, Saudi Arabia also warned that efficiency and complementarity must not become a justification for abandoning an established process. The group called for agreement on the continuation of the third and subsequent reviews, with their modalities and timeline to be discussed at the next COP meeting.

item.title: Xi hailed for bold vision on APEC progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
Amid ongoing geopolitical tensions and fragmentation, President Xi Jinping's emphasis on openness and economic cooperation, delivered in his speech at the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, carries far-reaching global implications and could provide significant impetus for globalization, international experts said. In the speech, Xi called for building an Asia-Pacific community characterized by solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, enterprise and innovation, as well as inclusive development. China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation, and it is ready to work with all parties to pool wisdom and synergy in building the four key pillars of an Asia-Pacific community, Xi said. He called for strengthening the pillar of economy and trade, upgrading the pillar of connectivity, fostering the pillar of innovation and enhancing the pillar of development. Jon R. Taylor, chair of the Department of Political Science and Geography at the University of Texas at San Antonio in the United States, said that Xi's speech offers a constructive framework for regional cooperation. Taylor noted that the four key pillars proposed by Xi for an Asia-Pacific community present a compelling vision for open regionalism, deeper economic integration and broader cooperation. These are hopeful signs that could spur greater efforts toward closer alignment of regional trade agreements, trade digitalization and reduced investment barriers, he said. "These sectors offer a rare combination of strong economic incentives and manageable political risks, making them the most likely areas where Xi's proposals can be translated into tangible results," he added. Adhere Cavince, a Kenyan scholar of international relations with a focus on China-Africa development cooperation, said the pillars outlined by President Xi could "significantly drive open trade, stable supply chains and a rules-based multilateral system". "Beyond the Asia-Pacific region, President Xi's remarks carry significant implications for Africa," Cavince said, noting that Xi's emphasis on economic and technological cooperation geared toward developing economies and infrastructure connectivity offers tangible channels for technology transfer, industrial upgrading and market access. "For the global economy, China casts itself as a stabilizer upholding (World Trade Organization) rules and predictability amid fragmentation," he said, emphasizing that China's proposals have the potential to reinforce globalization. Dicky Budiman, a senior researcher at both YARSI University in Indonesia and Griffith University in Australia, said the APEC meeting presents an important opportunity to reposition regional cooperation toward a more integrated, resilient and sustainable Asia-Pacific community. "President Xi's emphasis on solidarity, openness, innovation and inclusive development provides a relevant strategic foundation for addressing increasingly interconnected global challenges," he said. In his speech, Xi announced that in line with the needs of Asia-Pacific cooperation, China will set up cooperation institutions in areas such as digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of small and medium-sized enterprises to contribute to innovation-driven and green growth in the Asia-Pacific region. Lawrence Loh, a professor and director of National University of Singapore's Centre for Governance and Sustainability, said, "President Xi has articulated a bold vision outlining the next steps of continued progress for the Asia-Pacific community. "With China's posture as a responsible global node for connectivity and innovation, Asia-Pacific economies stand to gain by actively participating in the emerging series of newly enabled collaborative initiatives," he said. Luigi Gambardella, president of ChinaEU, a Brussels-based nonprofit international association that promotes Sino-European business cooperation in the digital sector, said that Xi's commitment to regional openness presents an important opportunity for Europe. "By connecting our respective industrial strengths and innovation ecosystems, we can create new sources of growth and competitiveness on both sides," Gambardella said. "The message from Shenzhen is powerful: Governments may compete, but their economies must remain connected." He added that "the significance of President Xi's speech lies not only in articulating a vision for the Asia-Pacific community, but also in proposing a concrete architecture to translate that vision into reality". Xu Weiwei in Hong Kong and Xing Yi in London contributed to this story.

item.title: Not quite as smooth as silk
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
The history of Chinese silk is, in many ways, a history of origins continually pushed further back in time. For decades, the earliest evidence of silk production seemed to lie in Neolithic textile fragments unearthed at sites such as Qianshanyang in Zhejiang province and Qingtai in Henan province, dating to roughly 6,000-4,000 years ago. Earlier still was the half-carbonized silkworm cocoon discovered in Xiyin village in Shanxi province in 1926, bearing traces of cutting that date to the Yangshao Culture period. That timeline shifted again in 2016. In a study published in the science journal Nature, researchers reported silk protein residues in soil samples from burials at the Jiahu site in Henan, dating back as far as 8,500 years. Along with weaving tools and bone needles unearthed there, the findings suggest that some of China's earliest Neolithic communities may already have possessed a basic knowledge of weaving and the deliberate use of silk fibers. The conclusion remains debated and awaits further material confirmation. Even so, the broader pattern is unmistakable: with each archaeological discovery, the beginnings of Chinese silk appear to recede ever deeper into prehistory. "That was an age when humans still lived in profound awe of the forces of nature — a world shaped by ritual, worship, and boundless imaginings about life and death," said Zhao Feng, a leading scholar of Chinese silk history and former director of the China National Silk Museum in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. That sense of awe still lingers in the objects left behind. Long before silk became a commodity, the silkworm itself appears to have occupied a place between nature, ritual, and myth. At the Shuanghuaishu site in Henan, archaeologists unearthed a 5,300-year-old ivory silkworm carved from a wild boar tusk. Depicting a silkworm spinning silk, the object is believed to have been associated with ritual practice or totemic worship, suggesting the silkworm had already acquired sacred significance in prehistoric China. Together with early silk remains found across the central Yellow River region, it points not only to the emergence of sericulture but also to a symbolic world built around silk. That world deepened over time. In ancient Chinese thought, the silkworm's life cycle — withdrawal into the cocoon, followed by transformation into a moth — came to symbolize metamorphosis, transcendence, and rebirth. A striking example survives in a jade artifact excavated from the Guo State cemetery in Henan, dating from the ninth to seventh centuries BC. Combining the body of a silkworm with the head of a dragon, it reveals how the silkworm entered the realm of cosmological imagination. Jade and gold silkworms were often buried with the dead, reflecting the belief that they could guide the soul toward transformation and eternity. By the Han Dynasty (206 BC-220 AD), silk had become both a pillar of imperial industry and a marker of cultural prestige. Vast state-run weaving workshops operated within the palace complexes of Chang'an (today's Shaanxi province), underscoring silk's central role in the empire's economy and political order. Weaving itself appears to have carried unusual social distinction. Historical accounts suggest that women associated with silk production could enjoy relatively elevated status, among them Consort Bo, mother of Emperor Wen, who was said to have once been a weaver before rising to imperial favor. The technological sophistication behind this industry became increasingly visible during the Han period. In 2012, archaeologists excavating Han tombs in Chengdu, Sichuan province, uncovered four wooden loom models accompanied by painted figurines of textile workers, vividly illustrating the complexity and specialization of early Chinese weaving. At least one model has been identified as a drawloom capable of producing intricate patterned silks such as brocade, making it the earliest surviving physical model of its kind discovered anywhere in the world. The discovery also underscored Sichuan province's long-standing role as a major silk production center. Decades of excavation at the Sanxingdui site in the province have yielded some of Bronze Age China's most iconic artifacts, including the towering Bronze Sacred Trees. According to Hu Jialin, the Shanghai Museum curator behind the well-publicized 2024 Sanxingdui exhibition, many scholars believe these extraordinary constructions represent Fusang, the mythical tree described in early texts as the resting place of the suns. Significantly, the character sang in Fusang means "mulberry" — the tree on which silkworms depend. "One of the things revealed by silk archaeology is the interconnected yet plural foundations of Chinese civilization," Zhao said. His view is reinforced by the discovery of several painted pottery spindle whorls dating back about 5,000 years across the central Yangtze River region — an area that would later give rise to the state of Chu (475-223 BC) and the broader Chu cultural tradition that long outlived it. Their varied forms, intricate patterns and carefully painted surfaces reveal a flourishing textile culture and, for some scholars, foreshadow the romantic, expansive spirit long associated with the Chu world. That spirit found one of its finest expressions in silk. Unearthed in 1982 from an aristocratic Chu tomb at Mashan in Hubei province, a gauze garment embroidered with dragon, phoenix and tiger motifs remains one of the masterpieces of ancient Chinese textile art. Though nearly two meters long, it weighs only about 250 grams; its gauze is woven so delicately that it has often been compared to cicada wings. Upon this almost weightless surface, artisans embroidered intricate motifs using brilliantly colored silk threads finer than human hair. The tomb yielded dozens of silk textiles preserved in astonishing condition by the dense white clay sealing the burial chamber. Separated by roughly two centuries yet linked by geography and cultural memory, the Mawangdui Han tombs in Changsha may be seen as heirs to this earlier Chu tradition. Among the most exquisite textiles unearthed there is a form of luxury needlework known as Xinqi embroidery. Recorded by name in the funerary inventories, it was celebrated for its extraordinarily fine stitching, harmonious colors and motifs worked with almost microscopic precision. At first glance, its flowing tassel-like cloud patterns appear abstract, but scholars believe they are stylized swallows woven among curling vines and drifting clouds. The symbolism was deeply resonant. Swallows are migratory birds that return unfailingly with the seasons, and the term xinqi — "faithful return" — alluded precisely to this cyclical homecoming. In the funerary imagination of Chu and early Han culture, the swallow became a metaphor for return itself: the return of spring, the return of memory, and perhaps even the hoped-for return of the soul.

item.title: Wuzhong's morning tea offers a savory warmup
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
A bowl of beef noodles, lamb offal soup, plates of braised meat, freshly fried pastries, dumplings and an assortment of cold dishes — breakfast in Wuzhong is anything but a simple meal. In Wuzhong, a city in Northwest China's Ningxia Hui autonomous region, tables are often filled with so many dishes that choosing where to begin can be a challenge. For Iraqi food vlogger and actor Ahmed Jaber, better known by his Chinese name Wang Lixuan, one local specialty proved particularly memorable. After trying hubo, a dish made by cutting flatbread into strips and stir-frying it with meat and seasonings, he was impressed by its chewy, tender texture and rich aroma. "Really satisfying. This is already on another level in terms of flavor," he said, after enjoying his meal at a local joint in Wuzhong. "I'll have another small portion, with some extra meat. The flavor is simply incredible." Sunday marked xiao xue, or Minor Snow, the 20th of China's"24 solar terms". As the weather turns colder, Wuzhong's morning tea offers a warming way to start the day. With steaming bowls of noodles, local meat dishes and bowls of Babao, or Eight Treasures, tea, Wuzhong's breakfast culture is hearty and down-to-earth, offering a robust alternative to the delicate dim sum of Cantonese morning tea. At the heart of the experience is Babao tea, traditionally served in a lidded bowl known as a gaiwan. Tealeaves form the base, while ingredients such as goji berries, red dates, sesame seeds, rose petals and walnuts add layers of flavor. Recipes vary from one establishment to another, and the tea is often refilled with hot water several times. The tea is meant to be enjoyed slowly. As the ingredients gradually release their flavors, each infusion brings a slightly different taste. The lid is used to gently brush aside the tea leaves and foam as people sip. Food is just as central to the experience. Wuzhong-style beef noodles are known for their rich, savory broth, made by simmering beef and beef bones. According to Hu Jiandong, a local researcher, the emphasis is on the beef itself, with the meat and broth served alongside the noodles. Lamb is another staple. Hand-grabbed lamb and lamb offal soup are common choices, while braised beef offers another meaty option. Local pastries add variety to the table, including youxiang, a fried dough snack, and flatbread flavored with locally grown perilla seeds. Fresh vegetables, sometimes served as simple cold dishes, provide a lighter contrast to the richer meat dishes. For Hu, the distinction between an ordinary breakfast and morning tea lies as much in the pace as in the food. "An ordinary breakfast is about eating quickly and getting on with the day. Morning tea means sitting down, having several dishes and pastries, and taking your time over a bowl of tea," he said. Although drinking tea at home has long been part of local life, gathering in restaurants for morning tea has become more established over the past decade. Older residents are often among the regular customers on weekdays, while weekends bring younger diners and families together. As Minor Snow settles in and the mornings grow colder, more people come in for hot soup, hot tea and hot food, Hu said. The end of the autumn harvest also gives residents more time to enjoy a leisurely breakfast.

item.title: From fading mining town to Xinjiang ski destination
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
When 13-year-old Qadir Hali arrived in Koktokay in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region in 1942, he could scarcely have imagined that the mining town would one day become a destination for skiers from across China and beyond. More than eight decades later, his son Kumash Qadir, now 63, has witnessed that transformation firsthand. Once a major mining center, Koktokay, in Xinjiang's Altay prefecture, is now home to one of China's earliest-opening ski resorts. Since launching its 2026-27 season on Oct 20, the resort has welcomed nearly 25,000 visitors, including more than 22,000 skiers, in the first two weeks. Mines fade, slopes rise Koktokay, meaning "green forest" in Kazakh, sits in the mineral-rich Altay Mountains. After mines were discovered in 1935, Koktokay earned a reputation as a major industrial center. But declining reserves and changing market demand brought economic hardship from the mid-to-late 1980s. The town's population fell from a peak of 50,000 to 60,000 to just over 10,000. Kumash, who was born in Koktokay, followed his father into the mining industry and worked there for 20 years. He recalled a thriving town where sporting events were regularly held. In 1999, as the mining industry declined, he lost his job. "As a local who grew up here, I felt quite lonely at the time and had little certainty about the future. Some people urged me to move away, but I had grown up here and felt attached to my hometown, so I wanted to stay," he said. To make a living, Kumash bought a car and began driving passengers between Koktokay and Urumqi, the regional capital. "Later the ski resort was built, and things slowly began to change," he recalled. The Koktokay International Ski Resort opened in 2020, providing Kumash with a new job on its operations team. His working day begins before dawn, when he drives his pickup truck to deliver safety nets to the slopes and anti-slip mats to the ski hall. In his spare time, he even helps care for a husky left with him by a skier. "Now I have a job, and the basics of life are taken care of," he said. "In the past, herders had little to do in winter, and the villages and town were quiet. Now there is winter work. Some people work at the resort, some serve tourists, and some rent out their houses for extra income." The tourism boom has also created opportunities for younger residents. Ardak Salinbek, 28, works at a ski equipment shop at an altitude of 2,200 meters, serving nearly 100 customers a day in winter. Born in Kairti Village, 15 kilometers from the resort, to a herder father and a farmer mother, she initially worked at a township hospital after graduating from medical school, earning less than 3,000 yuan ($425) a month. "The pay wasn't high, and the work was rather dull. I felt the ski-gear business suited me better. I get to meet friends from all over the country and learn something new every day," she said. Her parents initially questioned the career change but were convinced when she brought home her first monthly paycheck of 16,000 yuan. "As skiing in Koktokay became better known across the country, my parents realized it was a new opportunity for young people. They told me to 'go for it'," Salinbek recalled. "Skiing has changed my hometown beyond recognition, and I want to contribute to its development," she said. "For me, that means finding the right gear for every skier who comes."

item.title: Xi's APEC speech inspires optimism for new chapter in Asia-Pacific prosperity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
SHENZHEN -- Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, calling for further efforts to build an Asia-Pacific community and write a new chapter of the Asia-Pacific miracle. Experts said Xi's speech at the gathering outlined China's vision for a stronger, more integrated Asia-Pacific community, offering a roadmap for the region to build on the achievements of the past three decades. They also said it could help deepen regional cooperation, create new opportunities for shared development and contribute to peace, stability and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific and beyond. A SHARED VISION In his Thursday speech, Xi stressed that building an Asia-Pacific community requires solidarity and mutual assistance, openness and integration, enterprise and innovation, as well as inclusive development. These requirements are interconnected and mutually reinforcing, said Herbert Sima, director of the China Studies Center at the University of Auckland, noting they not only provide guidance for economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific, but also offer valuable insights into addressing global uncertainties. Solidarity and mutual assistance form the foundation of cooperation, openness and connectivity provide a pathway for development, innovation and progress serve as the driving force for growth, while inclusive development is key to ensuring that cooperation is sustainable and benefits all parties, the expert explained. In his speech, Xi reviewed the achievements of the Asia-Pacific miracle over the past thirty-plus years, stressing the need to adapt to the new realities, take new strides and open up new prospects for Asia-Pacific cooperation in the face of new opportunities and challenges. Xi's remarks have prompted experts to again reflect on the factors behind the region's remarkable economic growth and the prospects for its future development. Virdika Rizky Utama, executive director of the Jakarta-based think tank PARA Syndicate, said the Asia-Pacific miracle had been driven by open cooperation, trade and investment, and the integration of regional industrial and supply chains. What Xi stressed about building the Asia-Pacific community offered a response to the challenges facing the region and a vision for future cooperation, he said. The expert particularly noted Xi's mention of "open regionalism" in his speech, saying that for developing economies such as Indonesia, the concept means access to broader markets and more convenient connectivity. Tran Thi Hai Yen, a researcher at the Institute for European and Americas Studies at Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences, said Xi's vision comes at a timely moment, which addresses the four practical needs currently facing the Asia-Pacific region. As the rotating chair of APEC this year, she added, China has further clarified the direction of cooperation and underscored the urgency of accelerating joint efforts, helping translate long-term vision into concrete cooperation agendas. History proves that economies can prosper through trade with one another, and Xi reaffirmed the value of trade cooperation and open regionalism, said Craig Emerson, director of the Australia APEC Study Center. Such remarks are highly encouraging at a time when trade liberalization has faced growing skepticism in recent years, noted Emerson, a former Australian trade minister. "If the Asia-Pacific miracle of the past more than three decades was a story of economic growth achieved through openness and cooperation, the next 30 years should be a story of shared prosperity achieved through inclusiveness and win-win cooperation," said South Korean lawmaker Kim Tae-nyeon. "Economies in the Asia-Pacific region differ in terms of economic size, stages of development, history and culture, making the region highly diverse," he said. "This diversity should be regarded as a valuable resource. We should leverage our respective strengths, complement one another's weaknesses and turn these differences into new opportunities for cooperation." BUILDING PILLARS TOGETHER China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner in Asia-Pacific economic cooperation, and it is ready to work with all parties to pool wisdom and synergy in building the four key pillars of an Asia-Pacific community, Xi said in his speech. He also called for strengthening the pillar of economy and trade, upgrading the pillar of connectivity, fostering the pillar of innovation and enhancing the pillar of development. On the importance of connectivity, Alvaro Echeverria, director of the Asia Pacific Chamber of Commerce in Chile, said the call to upgrade the pillar of connectivity was particularly relevant in the current international environment. Greater proximity helps create mutual understanding, Echeverria told Xinhua, saying he welcomes China's call to strengthen connectivity not only through physical infrastructure, but also through continued efforts to promote human development and closer people-to-people exchanges. These efforts could help rebuild trust at a time when the world faces considerable uncertainty and a lack of predictability, while the need for international coordination continues to grow, he added. Xi pointed out that China is rooted in the Asia-Pacific and will continue to support Asia-Pacific cooperation, and announced that China will provide $20 million to support APEC's practical cooperation, and to establish a Center for Asia-Pacific Community Studies in Shenzhen to conduct policy research and exchanges and provide intellectual support. In addition, Xi said that in line with the needs of Asia-Pacific cooperation, China will set up cooperation institutions in such areas as digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to contribute to innovation-driven and green growth in the Asia-Pacific. China's proposal to set up cooperation institutions focusing on the digital economy, clean energy and SME cooperation carries great significance and represents a key step in fostering new growth drivers for the Asia-Pacific, said Vitaly Mankevich, president of the Russian-Asian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs. "As a recognized technology leader in the digital economy, clean energy and related sectors, China can use these cooperation bodies to advance pragmatic cooperation among Asia-Pacific economies and build science and technology innovation partnerships," Mankevich said. Georgie Too Hann Huei, COO of the Malaysia-China Business Council in Kuala Lumpur, said China is not only an active practitioner in the digital economy, clean energy and the development of SMEs, but has also accumulated rich experience in these fields, noting that China is now translating its development experience into concrete actions to promote common regional development. "This approach of 'getting its own house in order first and then bringing partners along' demonstrates China's leading role and exemplary influence in regional cooperation," he said.

item.title: Xi Story: Bringing Hainan's rainforest back to life
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
HAIKOU -- Zhou Zhaoli, a member of the Hainan gibbon monitoring team, starts his day at 4:30 am, long before sunrise. With flashlights in hand, he and his teammates pick their way through dense undergrowth in the mountainous Bawangling area of South China's Hainan province, braving thorns and leech bites. Their reward is sometimes the sight of Hainan gibbons high in the forest canopy, and the sound of their distinctive calls echoing through the trees at first light. The world's 20 gibbon species live in 11 Asian countries, and most are in decline. Native to the island province's tropical rainforests, the Hainan gibbon was once pushed to the brink of extinction by commercial logging, deforestation and poaching. Today it is the only gibbon species in the world whose population has kept growing. During an inspection tour of Hainan in April 2022, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited part of these rainforests and asked local villagers whether they had seen the rare primates. At that time, the habitat hosted 36 gibbons in five groups. By the end of 2025, the figure reached 44 gibbons in seven groups, up from fewer than 10 in two groups in the early 1980s. Hainan's tropical rainforest is China's largest, best-preserved and most concentrated stretch of contiguous island-type tropical rainforest. The rainforest was once fragmented across more than 20 nature reserves and other protected areas in nine cities and counties. In 2019, Hainan began piloting an integrated approach, placing previously separate nature reserves, forest parks and state-owned forest farms under unified management. About two years later, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park was established as one of China's first five national parks, which together span ecosystems from giant panda habitats in Sichuan, Gansu and Shaanxi provinces to the only home of the Hainan gibbon. Xi has closely followed the park's development. In 2018, he called for establishing national parks, including those protecting tropical rainforests. In 2019, he chaired a key reform meeting that approved a pilot plan for the Hainan national park. In 2021, he announced the establishment of China's first five national parks at the COP15 leaders' summit. During that 2022 inspection tour, Xi walked along a boardwalk in the national park, taking a close look at its natural environment. "He slowed his pace, studying the trees and listening closely to the sounds of nature as we walked," said Zheng Yan, a member of the park's public education and outreach team, who accompanied Xi and introduced the park to him during the visit. The park has improved markedly in both infrastructure and management capacity since its establishment, said Zheng, who has worked there for more than a decade. Xi's interest in rainforest conservation extends beyond China. On a visit to Brazil in July 2014, he recalled his 2009 trip to Manaus, a city deep in the Amazon rainforest, saying that protecting this vast expanse of pristine forest was vital to the global ecosystem. Protecting tropical rainforests is closely tied to humanity's survival and well-being, and it is a shared responsibility that calls for concerted global efforts. In recent years, China and Brazil have deepened cooperation on climate change and sustainable development. With support from the international community, the two countries are exploring new approaches to rainforest conservation and development, including measures that help local farmers improve their livelihoods and reduce deforestation while safeguarding the world's precious ecological assets and advancing global climate goals. Greice Quele Aparecida Barboza de Oliveira, an environmental analyst with Brazil's Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, visited Hainan recently to learn about China's approach to biodiversity conservation and to see how the national park protects the rare primate. "These are areas I knew little about before. I am studying them closely so that I can take China's experience in wildlife conservation home with me," she said. She was in Hainan for the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference, which ended on Sunday and drew international officials, experts and representatives from more than 20 countries. Climate change is becoming an increasingly serious challenge in Brazil and around the world, she said, adding that international cooperation and exchanges like those at the Hainan conference can help share effective conservation practices with other countries. During his 2022 visit to Hainan, Xi also asked about forest rangers' income and village-level public spending. He stressed the need to strictly protect tropical rainforests while ensuring that ecological conservation, green development and improvements in people's livelihoods go hand in hand. Hainan's tropical rainforest lies in one of the world's 34 biodiversity hotspots and serves as a reservoir of water, a source of food and wealth and a carbon sink. "Hainan's tropical rainforest does not belong to Hainan alone. It belongs to the people of the whole country and to Mother Earth as a whole. It is a national treasure," Xi said.
